Exact probabilistic inference · October 2026

tddlog, Dice, Alea.jl and Roulette

Exact inference systems on the benchmark programs of the papers on Dice, Alea.jl, bit blasting, Roulette and Geni. tddlog compiles ProbLog into tree decision diagrams; Dice compiles its own language into BDDs; Alea.jl compiles Julia programs into BDDs through CUDD, and HyBit is its bit blasting of continuous distributions; Roulette compiles Racket programs into BDDs by symbolic evaluation. Every answer is checked against an independent reference, except where one system alone answers (tddlog on 41 instances, Alea.jl on 5 instances), marked one answer in the tables. Of 485 instances, 37 that every system answers in under a second are left out, and so are 31 that no system ran, each system having failed on a smaller size of the same program; the plots and tables show the other 417.

Findings

Bit-blasted programs

tddlog alone answers genes up to 100 genes in 12 s, where Alea.jl times out at the paper's 5; fair_dt14 up to 32 bits in 71 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 20 (16 s) and times out at 24; fair_dt4 up to 32 bits in 72 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 20 (13 s) and times out at 24; addFun_max up to 29 bits in 51 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 21 (152 s) and runs out of memory at the paper's 23; clickGraph up to 16 bits in under a second, where Alea.jl answers up to 8 and runs out of memory at the paper's 10; tug_of_war up to 28 bits in under a second, where Alea.jl answers up to 20 (159 s) and times out at the paper's 22; addFun_sum up to 29 bits in 1.0 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 23 (432 s) and times out at 25; clinicalTrial2 up to 18 bits in under a second, where Alea.jl answers up to 12 (308 s) and runs out of memory at 14; conjugate_gaussians up to 29 bits in 1.5 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 23 (169 s) and times out at 25; pi up to 20 bits in 185 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 16 (334 s) and times out at 18; clinicalTrial1 up to 10 bits in 52 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 8 (263 s) and runs out of memory at 10; genes5 up to 27 bits in 10 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 25 (81 s) and runs out of memory at 27; normal_mixture_mu1 at the paper's precision (9 bits, 139 s), where Alea.jl answers up to 7 and runs out of memory at the paper's 9; normal_mixture_mu2 at the paper's precision (9 bits, 173 s), where Alea.jl answers up to 7 and runs out of memory at the paper's 9; zeroone_w2 up to 25 bits in 6.8 s, where Alea.jl answers up to 23 (326 s) and runs out of memory at 25; and normal_mixture_theta at the paper's precision (9 bits, 32 s), where Alea.jl runs out of memory at the paper's 9. Against Alea.jl's time without compilation, over the 162 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 5 550 s in all and Alea.jl 18 143 s; over the 135 both answer, 1 743 s against 4 369 s, and tddlog is faster on 64 of the 135 both answer; against Alea.jl's process, over the 162 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 5 550 s in all and Alea.jl 33 300 s; over the 135 both answer, 1 743 s against 18 755 s, and tddlog is faster on 134 of 135.

Where Alea.jl leads

On multimodal, a circuit of 4 617 random flips at its smallest size, tddlog runs out of memory at that size with each of its three vtrees and Alea.jl answers, in 31 s there. On conjugate_ex3 and laplace Alea.jl reaches 2 to 4 bits further than tddlog's best vtree. Of the 223 bit-blasted instances that some system ran, tddlog answers 199 (201 with one of its three vtrees), Alea.jl 141 and Dice 19.

The paper's samplers

At the paper's precision the exact answer is closer to the model's than any sampler comes in its runs on GPA (2e-16, which tddlog computes in 20 s; the closest sampler, WebPPL's MCMC with 104 samples, comes to 2e-3 in 208 s); tug_of_war (5e-7, which tddlog computes in 0.6 s; the closest sampler, Stan with 107 samples, comes to 4e-5 in 52 s); conjugate_gaussians (5e-6, which tddlog computes in 0.9 s; the closest sampler, WebPPL's rejection with 106 samples, comes to 2e-4 in 71 s); zeroone_w1 (9e-5, which tddlog computes in 0.3 s; the closest sampler, Stan with 105 samples, comes to 2e-1 in 102 s); zeroone_w2 (5e-4, which tddlog computes in 1.3 s; the closest sampler, Stan with 105 samples, comes to 1e-1 in 102 s); addFun_sum (4e-6, which tddlog computes in 0.7 s; the closest sampler, WebPPL's rejection with 106 samples, comes to 7e-4 in 7.3 s); clinicalTrial1 (5e-16, which tddlog computes in 1.7 s; the closest sampler, Stan with 106 samples, comes to 2e-3 in 311 s); clinicalTrial2 (7e-7, which tddlog computes in 0.02 s; the closest sampler, Stan with 107 samples, comes to 1e-4 in 87 s); and addFun_max (3e-7, which tddlog computes in 37 s; the closest sampler, WebPPL's MCMC with 107 samples, comes to 4e-4 in 68 s). On normal_mixture_mu1, normal_mixture_mu2, trueskill and conjugate_ex3 a sampler comes as close to the model as the exact answer at the paper's precision, sooner than the exact systems answer. Stan's HMC does not converge on altermu2, multimodal, zeroone_w1 and zeroone_w2: its error at its largest sample count stays above 1% of the answer.

Roulette's programs

tddlog reaches the largest size on caesar, diamond, the hmm's filtering joint, the hmm's filtering marginal, the hmm's marginal likelihood, the hmm's smoothing joint, the hmm's smoothing marginal, ladder, motivating and network, or ties and is fastest there. Dice reaches the largest size on hardware, or ties and is fastest there. On the nine networks tddlog answers 9, Roulette 9, Dice 8 and Alea.jl 9. In total time: against Roulette, over the 65 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 89 s in all and Roulette 15 118 s; over the 40 both answer, 3.8 s against 118 s; against Dice, over the 75 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 224 s in all and Dice 22 431 s; over the 40 both answer, 44 s against 1 431 s; and against Alea.jl, over the 71 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 112 s in all and Alea.jl 6 560 s; over the 61 both answer, 36 s against 560 s. Of the 88 instances that some system ran, tddlog answers 88, Roulette 40, Dice 40 and Alea.jl 61.

Geni's programs

tddlog leads on the grid, router failures: it answers up to 20×20 (4.5 s) and runs out of memory at 24×24, where Dice answers up to 16×16 (78 s) and times out at 18×18, Alea.jl answers up to 14×14 (101 s) and runs out of memory at 16×16 and ProbLog answers up to 6×6 (12 s) and times out at 8×8. Dice leads on the grid, link failures: it answers up to 16×16 (331 s) and times out at 18×18, where tddlog answers up to 14×14 (22 s) and runs out of memory at 16×16, Alea.jl answers up to 14×14 (132 s) and times out at 16×16 and ProbLog answers up to 6×6 (5.6 s) and times out at 8×8. tddlog leads on the weather factory, by factories: it answers up to 16 factories (18 s) and runs out of memory at 17 factories, where Dice answers up to 16 factories (385 s) and times out at 17 factories, Alea.jl answers up to 11 factories (216 s) and runs out of memory at 12 factories and ProbLog answers up to 2 factories (3.9 s) and runs out of memory at 7 factories. tddlog leads on the weather factory, by days: it answers every size run, up to 1000 days (65 s), where Dice answers every size run, up to 1000 days (381 s), Alea.jl answers up to 9 days (57 s) and runs out of memory at 100 days and ProbLog answers up to 5 days (51 s) and runs out of memory at 6 days. In total time: against Dice, over the 44 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 1 024 s in all and Dice 3 269 s; over the 42 both answer, 420 s against 2 338 s; against Alea.jl's time without compilation, over the 33 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 88 s in all and Alea.jl 4 363 s; over the 27 both answer, 27 s against 763 s; against its process, over the 33 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 88 s in all and Alea.jl 4 679 s; over the 27 both answer, 27 s against 1 079 s; and against ProbLog, over the 18 instances that either answers, a run that does not answer counted at the 600 s limit, tddlog takes 60 s in all and ProbLog 4 892 s; over the 10 both answer, 0.3 s against 92 s. Storm's dd engine answers the router grids up to 40×40, and PRISM from 24×24 to 40×40, where it finds the Markov chain's states too many for its sparse engine (8,925,478,909 at 24×24) and switches to its MTBDD engine. Both iterate the chain's values in doubles over decision diagrams rather than solve the chain, which stays small and fast only because every probability in these programs is within 6e-7 of 0.5; their answer, 0.50000045 at every size, is within 1e-6 of the reference and counts as an answer. The engines that solve the whole chain, Storm's exact and sparse ones and PRISM's sparse one, time out from 18×18 (Storm) and 20×20 (PRISM). Answers that differ from the references: merlin on geni_weather_h1 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h2 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h3 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h4 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h5 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h6 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h7 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h8 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_h9 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_n10 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_n11 (zero), geni on geni_weather_n12 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_n12 (zero), geni on geni_weather_n13 (zero), merlin on geni_weather_n13 (zero), geni on geni_weather_n15 (zero), geni on geni_weather_n16 (zero) and geni on geni_weather_n17 (zero); tddlog's agree to 1.2e-13 relative.

Answers

tddlog's answers agree with the references everywhere, to 4e-10 relative against Alea.jl and exact references and to 5e-8 against ProbLog's eight printed digits. ProbLog's d-DNNF is wrong on four bit-blasted circuits (clickGraph at 14 bits, by 0.016, pi at 12 bits, by 0.17, wmi_star at None bits, by 0.00022 and wmi_star at None bits, by 6.3e-05), which Ganak's exact count confirms. Dice prints 0 for every answer on 14 bit-blasted circuits, and Alea.jl's discretization is defective in the far tails of a normal, which moves the gene expression program's answer at Figure 2's precision from 1/2 to 0.333 with 5 genes and 0.482 with 20, where the artifact's own runs give 0.4999995 at every number of genes.

Bit-blasted programs

The programs of the bit-blasting paper (Garg, Holtzen, Van den Broeck and Millstein, PLDI 2024), from its artifact. HyBit, the paper's system, is Alea.jl's bit blasting: it replaces each continuous distribution by a distribution over fixed-point numbers, piecewise linear or exponential over a number of pieces, and compiles the program exactly. Each of the 19 programs of the paper's Table 2 runs at the paper's precision (marked paper in the table) and at 2, 4 and 6 bits after the point below and above it; the gene expression program of the paper's Figures 1 and 2 runs from 5 to 100 genes (the paper's 5 to 50) and, with 5 genes, by precision; the multimodal model and the conjugate Gaussians of Figures 3 and 5 run by precision. A size is the width of the program's numbers in bits. Table 2 of the paper gives each system's error within 20 minutes, not HyBit's time.

Alea.jl runs each program itself. tddlog and Dice run the Boolean circuit Alea.jl builds for it (its random flips and its gates, written as a ProbLog and a Dice program), so the three answer the same discrete program and must agree to rounding; Alea.jl's answer is the reference. Where Alea.jl fails, the reference is the circuit's exact weighted model count by Ganak in rational arithmetic where Ganak finishes (computed apart from the runs, untimed), and otherwise ProbLog's answer (its d-DNNF compilation). ProbLog's d-DNNF is wrong on clickGraph at 14 bits: it gives 0.6865 for the query e1(3) where Ganak's count and tddlog give 0.6706, with all queries or with that one alone. ProbLog's d-DNNF is wrong on pi at 12 bits: its answer is off Alea.jl's by 1.7e-1. ProbLog's d-DNNF is wrong on wmi_star at None bits: its answer is off Alea.jl's by 2.2e-4. ProbLog's d-DNNF is wrong on wmi_star at None bits: its answer is off Alea.jl's by 6.3e-5. An answer that no other system or count confirms is marked "one answer" in the table.

tddlog runs three ways: with its default, which tries a few vtrees in turn under bounds in diagram size that double each round and answers with the first to finish; with --vtree program, a variable order, as in a BDD, that reads the flips in the order the circuit lists them, the order in which Alea.jl made them; and with --vtree decision. A circuit that bit-blasts a distribution reads its selector flips in nested if-then-elses whose branches read the same flips again; for the decision vtree tddlog conditions each derived atom on the selector flips that guard it, so that a branch no longer reads them, and places each selector above the flips it decides between, so that the circuit is laid out as its own decision tree. On clickGraph, clinicalTrial1, clinicalTrial2, pi, wmi_path and wmi_star tddlog reads no flip of the smallest circuit as a guard: it has no decision vtree there (n/a), and the ladder stops.

On the gene expression program at 14 or more bits after the point, Alea.jl's discretization is defective: in the far upper tail of a normal distribution it takes the probability of a point as a difference of two values of the distribution function near 1, finer than doubles resolve there, and the reading of 136 lies 7 standard deviations up the normal of a patient without a gene. The circuit makes the readings far likelier without a gene than with one, where the model has them equally likely: 1.9e3 times at 14 bits and twice as much with each further bit, as the true probability of a point halves and the circuit's does not. The answer moves from the model's 1/2 toward 1/3, the first gene's expected probability given that it does not occur, as far as the prior probability that no gene occurs, 2−T, lets it: at Figure 2's precision, 20 bits after the point, 0.33338 with 5 genes, 0.48235 with 20 and 0.4999995, the mean of the prior's grid, from 50 genes; the artifact's own runs behind Figure 2 give 0.4999995 at every number of genes. Those circuits are marked in the table, and every exact system is scored against the circuit's own exact answer; on the genes circuits at Figure 2's precision only tddlog finishes, and its two arms, which agree, are the only check. The conjugate Gaussians of Figure 5 show the same effect, milder: their posterior lies about 5.7 standard deviations up the prior, and Alea.jl's answer moves away from the model's 17/3 as the precision grows, to 5.66653 at 10 bits after the point, 5.66330 at 14 and 5.65919 at 16.

Each point is one instance; below the diagonal tddlog is faster, and the dashed lines mark a factor of ten. A failure (timeout, out of memory) is drawn in the shaded band. Hover over a point for its name and times.

The paper's other systems — samplers and Psi on the continuous programs, beside the exact systems on the bit-blasted program at the paper's precision. The target is the error of the bit-blasted program's exact answer against the continuous model's answer; a sampler's cell gives the time it took to come as close (the median error over three seeds, at 102 or 103 to 107 samples, ten times more each run), or its smallest error where it never did. Not on the same footing: a sampler's error is a random variable, and the exact systems answer a discretized program.

  1. the artifact's Stan program truncates the hours at 0 only, not to [0, 8]; that model's answer is 0.33074 (Table 2 marks Stan unsupported here).
  2. the artifact's WebPPL program leaves out the truncation of the hours to [0, 8]; that model's answer is 0.38995.
  3. the artifact's WebPPL program puts hard constraints of the opposite sign in place of the 1/e penalty, and no weights meet them.
  4. the artifact's WebPPL program puts hard constraints of the opposite sign in place of the 1/e penalty and maps a two-argument function over one list, so every point gets the same label; that model's answer is 5.335.
  5. the artifact's WebPPL program maps a two-argument function over the pairs, so every observation reads as a failure; that model's answer is 1/7.

Roulette's programs

The scaling programs of the Roulette paper (Moy, Czenszak, Li, Marshall and Holtzen, PLDI 2025), from its artifact: a Markov chain, diamonds and ladders, a Caesar cipher, a hidden Markov model with five queries, a lossy network and an interpreter whose memory fails, each on a ladder from the artifact's sizes up to sizes where the systems run out of time, and its nine Bayesian networks. Roulette runs the artifact's own programs; tddlog and Dice run ProbLog and Dice programs of the same models with the same probabilities, and Alea.jl runs the Dice programs. The paper runs the network and the interpreter in Roulette only; the Dice programs here hold the message as a flag and four Booleans and unroll the interpreter's loop. The references are a dynamic program over each model's states (the clique tree on the networks).

Two things in the artifact (data/roulette/README.md): Roulette's default query takes one value's probability as one minus the others', which loses it once the evidence falls below about 1e-16 (on caesar it prints 0 for a key of probability 0.52 at 25 letters and 0.98 at 50); and its generator of the Dice caesar programs is a copy of the motivating program's, so the paper's Dice times on caesar are those of the Markov chain.

Each point is one instance; below the diagonal tddlog is faster, and the dashed lines mark a factor of ten. A failure is drawn in the shaded band. 0 of these instances are answered by every system in under a second and are left out.

How far each system reaches — per program the largest size a system answers within 600 s and its time there, else its failure at the smallest size; the furthest is marked

Geni's programs

The programs of Geni's evaluation (Li and Zhang, “Compiling with Generating Functions”, ICFP 2025) that Dice runs, as its artifact writes them. The grid networks of its Figure 11: an N×N grid of routers whose links each work with probability 0.5, after the grid on which Fierens et al. evaluated ProbLog, the probability that a packet from the top-left router reaches the bottom-right one; and a grid whose routers each work with a probability that depends on whether their left and upper neighbours work. And the weather factory of its Figure 9, a Markov chain translated to Dice by Rubicon (Holtzen et al., CAV 2021): the probability that all of n factories, whose strikes depend on the day's weather, are on strike within h days, by n at 10 days and by h with 10 factories. Each is a Dice program, translated to ProbLog for tddlog and ProbLog (its d-DNNF compilation, which here runs beside the others) and to Julia for Alea.jl; Geni itself is not run. The references come from a dynamic program over each model's states.

Each point is one instance; below the diagonal tddlog is faster, and the dashed lines mark a factor of ten. A failure is drawn in the shaded band. 4 of these instances are answered by every system in under a second and are left out.

All programs

The bit-blasted programs, Roulette's programs and Geni's programs together with the arithmetic programs of Cao et al., Pluck's sequence models, noDice's programs, the Dice paper's loop programs unrolled to growing sizes, its networks and its example programs, for every system that ran any of them: an instance a system did not answer counts as unanswered, whether it failed or the system was not given it. Dice's times on the bit-blasted programs; Roulette's times on the bit-blasted programs and ppl; Geni's times on the bit-blasted programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; noDice's times on the bit-blasted programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs; Psi's times on the bit-blasted programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs; Genfer's times on the bit-blasted programs and Geni's programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; SPPL's times on the bit-blasted programs and Geni's programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; Pluck's times on Geni's programs and Roulette's programs and std; Storm sparse's times on the bit-blasted programs and Geni's programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; Storm exact's times on the bit-blasted programs and Geni's programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; Storm dd's times on the bit-blasted programs and Geni's programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; PRISM sparse's times on the bit-blasted programs and Geni's programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; PRISM hybrid's times on the bit-blasted programs and Geni's programs and loops and ppl and Roulette's programs and std; ProbLog's times on the bit-blasted programs and Roulette's programs come from another run than tddlog's and are left out of these plots. 37 of the 485 instances are answered by every system in under a second, and 31 lie beyond the sizes at which every system failed; both are left out.

  • Pluck was not given 264 of the 417 instances: it runs only its own programs.

Programs by family

Seconds, the median of the repetitions; the fastest answer of a row is marked. A failure gives its kind: >600 a timeout, memout out of memory (or ended by the machine's out-of-memory guard when the lanes together ran its memory low), skipped not run after a failure on a smaller instance of the same program. zero: every answer printed 0 though a double holds the answers and the evidence (Dice drops evidence below 1e-6); underflow: every answer printed 0 where the answers or the evidence are below the smallest double; wrong: an answer off the reference by more than 1e-6. None of the three is counted as an answer in the plots. The last column is the largest relative difference of any system's answers from the reference.

Answers

Every answer is checked against a reference that another system or method computes: Alea.jl's answer on the Alea.jl programs and the bit-blasted circuits, Ganak's exact count of a circuit where Alea.jl fails, ProbLog's d-DNNF (which prints eight digits) on the Dice programs, the clique tree on the networks, and a dynamic program over the model's states on Roulette's and Geni's programs; where none answers, the system that does is the reference of the others, and an answer that nothing confirms is marked "one answer" in the tables. A cell gives the instances whose answers agree with the reference to 1e-6, absolute or relative, the largest difference among them (relative, or absolute where only that is within 1e-6), and the instances where the system prints an answer that does not agree: zero, every answer printed as 0 though the reference's are positive and the evidence's probability is a double; underflow, the same where the evidence's probability is below the smallest double; wrong, an answer off by more.

Ace c2d is off the reference on the bit-blasted wmi_star_n128 (by inf), wmi_star_n256 (by inf), wmi_star_n512 (by inf) and clinicalTrial1 (6 by inf, 8 by inf, 10 by inf); and the Dice paper's scaled diamond (1600 by inf): Ace through c2d (-forceC2d) prints NaN for every marginal, where its default route, a tabular compilation, answers right; the cause is not known. aspmc prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's hmm_filtering_joint (1000), hmm_filtering_marginal (1000), hmm_smoothing_joint (1000) and hmm_smoothing_marginal (1000): the evidence's probability is below the smallest double. aspmc prints 0 for every answer on the bit-blasted clinicalTrial1 (6): aspmc reports the evidence inconsistent, though its probability is positive. Dice prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's caesar (200, 300, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000), hmm_filtering_joint (1000), hmm_filtering_marginal (1000, 3000, 10000), hmm_smoothing_joint (1000) and hmm_smoothing_marginal (1000, 3000, 10000); the arithmetic caesar_huge; and the Dice paper's scaled caesar-iter (3000) and simpleCaesar (300, 1000): the evidence's probability is below the smallest double. Dice is off the reference on Roulette's bn_insurance (by 7.4e-6); noDice's insurance (by 7.4e-6); and the Dice paper's bn_insurance (by 7.4e-6) and bn_pathfinder (by 4.5e-5): Dice drops most values of a discrete below 1e-4. Dice prints 0 for every answer on the bit-blasted markov_n10, weekend_p1024, weekend_p16, weekend_p256, weekend_p4, weekend_p64, clinicalTrial1 (4, 6), genes5 (17) and weekend (22, 24, 26, 28, 30); Roulette's caesar (25, 50, 100), hmm_filtering_joint (100, 300), hmm_filtering_marginal (100, 300), hmm_smoothing_joint (100, 300) and hmm_smoothing_marginal (100, 300); the arithmetic caesar_large, caesar_medium and caesar_small; the Dice paper's digitRecognition; and the Dice paper's scaled caesar-iter (100, 1000) and simpleCaesar (100): Dice answers 0 wherever the evidence's probability is below 1e-6. Geni is off the reference on Roulette's bn_munin (by 3.0e-4): Geni rebuilt in double precision gives the same answers, so its rounding does not explain them, and every row of the program's tables sums to one; whether Geni or the program dice2geni.py writes is at fault is not known. Geni is off the reference on Roulette's network (1000 by 1.4e-6, 3000 by 2.7e-6): Geni computes in single precision, whose rounding adds up along these programs' chains of diamonds. Geni is off the reference on the Dice paper's scaled diamond (400 by 3.0e-6, 1600 by 1.2e-5, 6400 by 4.0e-5) and ladder (1600 by 1.9e-6): Geni computes in single precision, whose rounding adds up along these programs' long chains. Geni prints 0 for every answer on Geni's weather_n (12, 13, 15, 16, 17): Geni prints seven decimals, and these answers are below 5e-8. Merlin prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's hmm_filtering_joint (1000), hmm_filtering_marginal (1000), hmm_marginal_likelihood (900), hmm_smoothing_joint (1000) and hmm_smoothing_marginal (1000); and the Dice paper's scaled simpleCaesar (300): the evidence's probability is below the smallest normal double: Merlin finds the evidence inconsistent or prints 0. Merlin prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's hmm_filtering_joint (100, 300), hmm_marginal_likelihood (100, 300, 600) and hmm_smoothing_joint (100, 300); Geni's weather_h (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) and weather_n (10, 11, 12, 13); and Pluck's hmm: Merlin prints six decimals, and these answers are below 5e-7. noDice prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's hmm_marginal_likelihood (900): noDice prints six decimals, and this answer is below 5e-7. noDice is off the reference on Roulette's hmm_filtering_joint (1000 by 5.0e-1), hmm_filtering_marginal (1000 by 1.2e-1), hmm_smoothing_joint (1000 by 5.0e-1) and hmm_smoothing_marginal (1000 by 5.0e-2); and the Dice paper's scaled simpleCaesar (300 by 5.0e-1): the evidence's probability is below the smallest double, and noDice prints 0.5 for every value. noDice prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's hmm_filtering_joint (100, 300), hmm_marginal_likelihood (100, 300, 600) and hmm_smoothing_joint (100, 300); noDice's 3sat-0; and Pluck's string_editing: noDice prints six decimals, and these answers are below 5e-7. PITA is off the reference on the bit-blasted linreg (8 by 9.5e-3); and the Dice paper's scaled caesar-iter (100 by 1.0e+0): the evidence's probability is below about 1e-16, which PITA loses: it evaluates a complemented edge of its diagrams as one minus its probability, in doubles. PITA is off the reference on Roulette's hmm_filtering_marginal (100 by 8.1e-1): PITA prints 1.43 for this conditional probability, above one, where it answers the smoothing programs of the same length right; the cause is not known. PITA is off the reference on the arithmetic caesar_small (by 3.1e-2): the evidence's probability is 5e-15, and PITA's probabilities of the query and the evidence together come out as multiples of 2-53, the spacing of doubles below one. ProbLog's d-DNNF is off the reference on the bit-blasted clickGraph (14 by 1.6e-2): Ganak's exact count of the circuit agrees with tddlog. ProbLog's d-DNNF is off the reference on the bit-blasted wmi_star_n16 (by 2.2e-4), wmi_star_n32 (by 6.3e-5) and pi (12 by 1.7e-1): Alea.jl, tddlog and aspmc give the same answer. Roulette prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's caesar (300, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000), hmm_filtering_joint (1000), hmm_filtering_marginal (1000, 3000), hmm_smoothing_joint (1000) and hmm_smoothing_marginal (1000, 3000); and the Dice paper's scaled caesar-iter (3000) and simpleCaesar (300): the evidence's probability is below the smallest double. Roulette, #f prints 0 for every answer on Roulette's caesar (300, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000): the evidence's probability is below the smallest double. SPPL is off the reference on the bit-blasted markov_n10 (by 6.7e-3), markov_n100 (by 1.8e-3), markov_n20 (by 6.9e-4) and markov_n50 (by 3.9e-4): SPPL runs its own program, exact on the continuous model, whose normal emissions the circuit rounds to a grid.

On GPA_w19, genes5_w17, genes_t5, markov_n10, population_s1 and weekend_w18, the network tools' failures are the harness's: ground2net.py, which writes the circuit's network, refused a fact row [1-p, p] whose sum is 1.00000000000000026, and the skip rule then left out the larger circuits of each family.

On the networks of the tables (not on this page): the other network tools' answers against the same references: pyAgrum 222 marginal runs to 2.0e-7 and 235 partition functions to 2.1e-7 in log10; pgmpy 136 marginal runs to 4.7e-9 and 214 partition functions to 2.2e-7 in log10; libDAI 231 marginal runs to 5.0e-7 and 262 partition functions to 2.2e-7 in log10; TensorInference.jl 355 marginal runs to 5.0e-7 and 390 partition functions to 2.2e-7 in log10 (the tools print six digits, as Merlin does).

How the numbers were taken

Machine
Three machines: a cloud machine with 96 physical cores and 1488 GB of memory, for the Alea.jl and noDice programs and the bit-blasted programs; a cloud machine with 96 physical cores and 1488 GB of memory, for the Dice paper's programs and Geni's programs and Roulette's programs; and a lab machine with 16 physical cores and 125 GB of memory, for the earlier run of Dice, ProbLog's references and the samplers on the bit-blasted programs. A run is one job that holds its machine alone. Programs run as independent jobs in lanes, each pinned to one logical CPU on its own physical core, with the machine's memory split between the lanes. In a lane all systems run on an instance back to back, in an order rotated by instance and repetition, so that the systems share the lanes alike.
Runs
The release run, all of its parts at one version of tddlog, each part with all of its systems in the same lanes: the arithmetic, sequence and noDice programs (60 lanes, 24 GB a process, three repetitions, 600 s, on the machine with 96 physical cores and 1488 GB of memory, 2026-10-19); the networks, the Dice paper's programs and the loop programs (94 lanes, 15 GB a process, three repetitions, 300 s for the networks and the Dice paper's programs and 600 s for the loop programs, on the machine with 96 physical cores and 1488 GB of memory, 2026-10-19); Roulette's programs (52 lanes, 28 GB a process, three repetitions, 600 s, on the machine with 96 physical cores and 1488 GB of memory, 2026-10-19); the bit-blasted programs for tddlog and Alea.jl (45 lanes, 33 GB a process, three repetitions, 600 s, on the machine with 96 physical cores and 1488 GB of memory, 2026-10-19); and Geni's programs, with ProbLog's d-DNNF timed beside the others (49 lanes, 30 GB a process, three repetitions, 600 s, on the machine with 96 physical cores and 1488 GB of memory, 2026-10-19). Dice, ProbLog's references and the samplers on the bit-blasted programs come from an earlier run (5 lanes, 25 GB a process, three repetitions, 600 s, 2026-10-12) on the same circuits; neither those systems nor the circuits have changed since. Times compare within a run: on the bit-blasted programs the plots show tddlog and Alea.jl, and Dice's times are in the tables only. The plots of all programs put the runs together.
Ladders
A program with a size runs from small to large, and a system that fails on one size (a timeout, out of memory, a crash) is not run on the larger sizes of that program; the tables mark those skipped, and they count as failures.
Repetitions
A time is the median of the repetitions, a failed repetition counted as longer than any time: of three repetitions, a system must answer in two.
What a time includes
For tddlog and Dice, the wall time of the process: parsing, compiling and answering every query. For Alea.jl, the time the program reports for building the model and computing its answers a second time in the same process, without Julia's compilation, as the papers time it; the process's wall time, with Julia's start-up, loading Alea.jl and compiling its methods, is the dashed line in the plots and the "process" column in the tables. For Roulette, the time the artifact's own time reports for building and querying the program; the dashed line adds Racket's start-up and loading.
Versions
tddlog 0.1.0 (Rust 1.94.0, linked statically), one version for every part of the release run, which gave both its times and its answers, printed with 17 digits after the point. Dice 1.0 (the binary of the sholtzen/dice image), with an unlimited stack. Alea.jl at revision cf5e5b8 on Julia 1.11.9 with CUDD 3.0.0 and Distributions.jl 0.25.131, one thread. Roulette from its PLDI 2025 artifact (revision 54d6185 of its repository) on Racket 8.16, the paper's Racket being 8.13 (baselines.md, section 11). ProbLog 2.3.0 with -k ddnnf, timed on Geni's programs, a clique-tree solver and dynamic programs over the models' states as references, and for the bit-blasted circuits that Alea.jl does not answer, exact weighted model counts by Ganak in rational arithmetic.
Further systems
Geni (gennifer; Li and Zhang, ICFP 2025), noDice (Gürtler and Kaminski, OOPSLA 2026), Psi (Gehr et al., CAV 2016; revision ef8a9e5), Genfer (Zaiser, Murawski and Ong, NeurIPS 2023), SPPL 2.0.4 (Saad, Rinard and Mansinghka, PLDI 2021), Pluck (Bowers et al., PLDI 2025), PITA (cplint, SWI-Prolog 9.2.9), aspmc 1.1.1 with sharpSAT-TD, Storm 1.14 (stormpy), one Sylvan thread (sparse, exact, dd), PRISM 4.8.1 (sparse, hybrid), Ace 3.0 (auto, forceC2d), Merlin 1.7.0's bucket-tree elimination (-a bte), pyAgrum's junction tree, pgmpy's variable elimination, libDAI's junction tree and TensorInference.jl's tensor network contraction (greedy, treesa). Their versions are those of docs/baselines.md.
Samplers
CmdStan 2.32.2 (the paper's 2.28.2 does not build both of the artifact's array syntaxes), WebPPL 0.9.15 on node 18, and Psi at revision ef8a9e5, each on the artifact's own program of the model, in the earlier run, three seeds. AQUA and GuBPI were installed but not timed (baselines.md, section 10): the artifact's AQUA inputs crash it or answer other quantities on all but four programs, and GuBPI's repository has programs for three of the models and prints bounds rather than an answer. Mathematica, with which the paper simplified Psi's integrals, is not available. Some of the artifact's sampler programs encode another model than the HyBit program: Stan's and WebPPL's weekend, and WebPPL's clinicalTrial2 and zeroone. The table marks them "another model" and gives, in a note, the answer of the model each encodes, worked out by hand; it is the value their estimates settle on.
